metadata.description: Medical thresholds and hazard indicators for deep space missions. Filled by the Research Lead from NASA, peer-reviewed and clinical sources. Same structure as the placeholder file.

research_notes.how_to_read_zones: Inside baseline_min..baseline_max = normal. Outside baseline but inside warning = caution. Beyond warning = warning. Beyond critical = critical. A null bound means that side does not apply.
research_notes.personal_baseline: NASA publishes no universal heart rate or blood pressure limit for astronauts. Where possible, compare each astronaut to their own baseline, and use these fixed values as a safety net.
research_notes.evidence_grades: A = NASA standard, NASA report or peer-reviewed. B = clinical reference or reputable secondary. TEAM = our design choice, not a NASA number.
research_notes.optional_fields: evidence_grade, direction and notes are extra. Delete them if the code does not need them.
research_notes.disclaimer: Screening and decision support only. Not a medical diagnosis.

heart_rate.hazard: Resting heart rate that rises can signal illness, dehydration, stress, poor sleep or CO2 effects. Over months, microgravity also causes cardiovascular deconditioning.
heart_rate.recommended_action: Recheck after 5 minutes at rest and compare with the astronaut's own baseline. Check hydration, sleep, CO2 and symptoms. Report to the medical officer if it stays high, drops below 40, or comes with chest pain or fainting. Keep the daily exercise plan to limit deconditioning.
heart_rate.evidence_grade: B for 60 to 100 (clinical reference). TEAM for warning and critical values. NASA has no universal limit.
heart_rate.notes: Resting adult range 60 to 100 bpm; fit people can sit near 40 without problems. In a NASA ISS study heart rate stayed the same in space while blood pressure fell, so use percent change from personal baseline (+10 percent yellow, +20 percent red) alongside these fixed values.

blood_pressure_sys.hazard: Fluid shifts toward the head. In ISS astronauts 24-hour blood pressure ran about 8 to 10 mmHg lower than on Earth while cardiac output rose 35 to 41 percent, which may be linked to vision changes (SANS). Low pressure raises fainting risk, especially after landing.
blood_pressure_sys.recommended_action: Recheck seated at rest. If low: lie down and drink fluids. If high: rest and recheck after 5 minutes. Report to the medical officer if it persists. Lower body negative pressure is an experimental fluid-shift countermeasure, not a treatment for abnormal blood pressure.
blood_pressure_sys.evidence_grade: A for the in-flight change. B for AHA categories (normal under 120/80, stage 1 starts 130, stage 2 starts 140, low 90/60 or under). TEAM for 85 and 70.
blood_pressure_sys.notes: Expect an astronaut who is 115/75 on Earth to read about 105/66 in flight. Emergency level on Earth is 180 over 120 or higher (hypertensive crisis). The nightly blood pressure dip is preserved in space.

blood_pressure_dia.hazard: Changes in fluid distribution and vessel relaxation in microgravity lower diastolic pressure in flight. Sustained high readings strain the heart and vessels.
blood_pressure_dia.recommended_action: Recheck seated at rest. Check fluid intake and salt intake. Report to the medical officer if readings stay outside the baseline range or come with dizziness, headache or vision changes.
blood_pressure_dia.evidence_grade: A for the in-flight drop (about 9 mmHg). B for AHA categories (stage 1 is 80 to 89, stage 2 is 90 or more, low is 60 or under). TEAM for 55, 40 and 85.
blood_pressure_dia.notes: Changed critical_high from 95 to 90 so it matches the AHA stage 2 start.

sleep_hours.hazard: Circadian rhythm disruption and sleep loss. NASA schedules 8.5 hours but ISS crews average about 6.1 hours. Under 6 hours is linked to worse attention and more mistakes. Sunrise happens every 90 minutes in orbit.
sleep_hours.recommended_action: Protect the sleep schedule, adjust cabin lighting to follow an Earth-like day, cut night workload, limit sleep medicine, and avoid safety-critical tasks after bad nights. Confirm with the 3-minute reaction test (lapse is 355 ms or more).
sleep_hours.evidence_grade: A for 8.5 scheduled, 6.09 real average and the 355 ms lapse rule. TEAM for 4.0, 10 and 12.
sleep_hours.notes: Use a 3-night rolling average. An astronaut at 6 to 7 hours is below target but matches the typical ISS average. Very long sleep has no NASA threshold; it is a TEAM flag for possible illness or low mood.

co2_mmhg.hazard: CO2 buildup causes headache, drowsiness and poor concentration, and at high levels danger to life. It can pool around a person when air fans stop.
co2_mmhg.recommended_action: Turn fans on, check the CO2 scrubber, move the person to fresher air, and report to the commander. Escalate and follow the emergency procedure if it keeps rising.
co2_mmhg.evidence_grade: A. NASA-STD-3001 limit is 3 mmHg (1-hour average). ISS crews reported symptoms from 2.3 mmHg. A NASA model reached about 10 mmHg after about 2 hours with ventilation off.
co2_mmhg.notes: 1 mmHg is about 1,316 ppm. The ISS 24-hour operational limit has been 4.0 mmHg.

o2_partial_pressure_mmhg.hazard: Too little oxygen causes confusion and fainting. Too much oxygen raises fire risk long before it becomes a medical problem.
o2_partial_pressure_mmhg.recommended_action: Check the oxygen supply and cabin pressure, move the crew member to a safe area if low, report to the commander, and treat any rise as a fire hazard.
o2_partial_pressure_mmhg.evidence_grade: A for 145 to 155 (normoxia target), 127 (mild hypoxia lower limit, accepted for about 1 week) and 356 (indefinite hyperoxia upper limit), from NASA-STD-3001 Vol 2 Rev B as shown in NASA slides. TEAM for 135.
o2_partial_pressure_mmhg.notes: PIO2 = (total pressure minus 47) times the oxygen fraction. At 101.3 kPa and 21 percent oxygen, PIO2 is about 150 mmHg. Newer revisions of the standard exist; check Table 6.2-1 before final submission.

radiation_total_msv.hazard: Long-term cancer risk, and possible effects on brain, heart and eyes.
radiation_total_msv.recommended_action: Track the running total, reduce time outside shielded areas, and plan remaining missions against the 600 mSv career limit.
radiation_total_msv.evidence_grade: A for 600 mSv (NASA-STD-3001 [V1 4030]). TEAM for 300 (50 percent) and 480 (80 percent).
radiation_total_msv.notes: Measured dose rates: 1.84 mSv per day on the cruise to Mars, 0.64 on the Mars surface. At 1.84 per day, 600 mSv is reached in about 326 days.

radiation_event_msv.hazard: Solar particle storms can cause nausea, vomiting and fatigue at high doses.
radiation_event_msv.recommended_action: Move to the shielded storm shelter, stay until the all-clear, track the dose and report to the commander.
radiation_event_msv.evidence_grade: A for 250 mSv (NASA design reference storm, a vehicle requirement) and for the measured 19.5 mSv event. TEAM for 100.
radiation_event_msv.notes: The three storms Curiosity measured on its cruise totalled 24.7 mSv, the largest 19.5 mSv.

stress_score.hazard: Isolation and confinement can lower mood and teamwork. NASA lists a formal Behavioral Health Risk and says Moon and Mars countermeasures are not yet validated.
stress_score.recommended_action: Offer a private check-in, protect rest and exercise, rotate tasks, and arrange a call with ground support (delayed on Mars). Escalate to the commander or medical officer for hopelessness or severe agitation.
stress_score.evidence_grade: A for the risk and the finding that mood falls over time. TEAM for the 0 to 10 scale and all numbers. NASA uses validated scales (POMS, BDI-II).
stress_score.notes: Also flag a falling mood trend over 14 days even when today's score looks fine.
